quote: In July, we announced 40 million messages a day, in December we announced 100 million, and as of this blog post we are well past 120 million.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy
note: Per day.

quote: We decided early on to store all chat history forever so users can come back at any time and have their data available on any device.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: The messages were stored in a MongoDB collection with a single compound index on channel_id and created_at.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy
note: Text continues: around November 2015 they reached 100 million stored messages.

quote: It quickly became clear that our reads were extremely random and our read/write ratio was about 50/50.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: Cassandra was the only database that fulfilled all of our requirements. We can just add nodes to scale it and it can tolerate a loss of nodes without any impact on the application.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: Cassandra is an AP database which means it trades strong consistency for availability which is something we wanted.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

claim: Partition key channel_id; Snowflake as clustering key
quote: channel_id became the partition key since all queries operate on a channel, but created_at didn't make a great clustering key because two messages can have the same creation time.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: Luckily every ID on Discord is actually a Snowflake (chronologically sortable), so we were able to use them instead. The primary key became (channel_id, message_id), where the message_id is a Snowflake.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

claim: Time buckets of about 10 days, under 100MB
quote: We decided to bucket our messages by time. We looked at the largest channels on Discord and determined if we stored about 10 days of messages within a bucket that we could comfortably stay under 100MB.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: our new primary key became ((channel_id, bucket), message_id).
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: We are currently running a 12 node cluster with a replica factor of 3 and will just continue to add new Cassandra nodes as needed.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: At the beginning of 2022, it had 177 nodes with trillions of messages.
author: Bo Ingram

quote: We're going from running 177 Cassandra nodes to just 72 ScyllaDB nodes.
author: Bo Ingram

claim: Request coalescing in Rust data services
quote: If multiple users are requesting the same row at the same time, we'll only query the database once.
author: Bo Ingram

quote: For example, fetching historical messages had a p99 of between 40-125ms on Cassandra, with ScyllaDB having a nice and chill 15ms p99 latency, and message insert performance going from 5-70ms p99 on Cassandra, to a steady 5ms p99 on ScyllaDB.
author: Bo Ingram

quote: (paraphrase, not verbatim) Rust migrator reached up to 3.2 million messages per second; migration finished in nine days.
author: Bo Ingram
note: Numbers came from a summarising fetch; exact wording not copied. Re-check before quoting.

quote: Fast forward two years, and we are up to nearly five million concurrent users and millions of events per second flowing through the system.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: Users connect to a WebSocket and spin up a session process (a GenServer), which then communicates with remote Erlang nodes that contain guild (internal for a “Discord Server”) processes (also GenServers).
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: When anything is published in a guild, it is fanned out to every session connected to it. When a user comes online, they connect to a guild, and the guild publishes a presence to all other connected sessions.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: Eventually we ended up with many Discord servers like /r/Overwatch with up to 30,000 concurrent users.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

quote: This meant that during peak hours, publishing an event from a large guild could take anywhere from 900ms to 2.1s!
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy

claim: Manifold: batch sends per remote node
quote: Manifold distributes the work of sending messages to the remote nodes of the PIDs (Erlang process identifier), which guarantees that the sending processes at most only calls send/2 equal to the number of involved remote nodes.
author: Stanislav Vishnevskiy
note: Last word 'nodes' inferred from context; the extract cut at 'remote'.

quote: Every Slack client has a persistent websocket connection to Slack's servers to receive real-time events
author: Sameera Thangudu

quote: Channel Servers (CS) are stateful and in-memory, holding some amount of history of channels. ... mapped to a subset of channels based on consistent hashing
author: Sameera Thangudu
note: Two fragments joined with '...'; wording from a summarising fetch, check exact sentence before quoting.

quote: (fragments) 'stateful and in-memory. They hold users' information and websocket channel subscriptions' and are 'the interface between Slack clients and CSs'
author: Sameera Thangudu
note: Fragments from a summarising fetch.

quote: (fragments) Admin Servers are 'stateless and in-memory' and 'interface between our Webapp backend and CSs'; Presence Servers are 'in-memory and keep track of which users are online' (the green presence dots).
author: Sameera Thangudu
note: Fragments from a summarising fetch.

quote: Webapp then sends that message to AS. AS looks at the channel ID in this message, discovers CS through a consistent hash ring, and routes the message to the appropriate CS that hosts the real time messaging for this channel. When CS receives the message for that channel, it sends out the message to every GS across the world that is subscribed to that channel. Each GS that receives that message sends it to every connected client subscribed to that channel id.
author: Sameera Thangudu

quote: At peak times, about 16 million channels are served per host
author: Sameera Thangudu

quote: our system delivers messages across the world in 500ms
author: Sameera Thangudu

quote: Slack sends millions of messages every day across millions of channels
author: Sameera Thangudu

quote: tens of millions of connected clients
author: Sameera Thangudu
note: Fragment.

quote: a new CS is ready to serve traffic in under 20 seconds
author: Sameera Thangudu
note: CHARM = Consistent Hash Ring Managers.

quote: An application-level caching service developed in-house and deployed to our edge points-of-presence.
author: Bing Wei
note: Caches user/channel/team data at the edge so clients lazy-load instead of loading everything at startup (rtm.start).

quote: Flannel has been running in our edge locations since January. It serves 4 million simultaneous connections at peak and 600K client queries per second.
author: Bing Wei

quote: on a 1.5K user team, it reduced the data size by 7 times; on a 32K user team, it was reduced by 44 times
author: Bing Wei
note: From a summarising fetch.

quote: Today we have an update for those keeping score at home: we are now able to easily push our systems to over 2 million tcp connections!!
author: WhatsApp (unsigned blog post)
note: Output shown: kern.ipc.numopensockets: 2277845. Hardware per summary: 24-core Xeon X5675, 103GB RAM, FreeBSD 8.2, Erlang R14B03.

quote: Best part is that we are able to do it with plenty of CPU and memory to spare and do it sustainably
author: WhatsApp (unsigned blog post)

quote: The WebSocket Protocol enables two-way communication between a client running untrusted code in a controlled environment to a remote host that has opted-in to communications from that code.
author: I. Fette, A. Melnikov (IETF)

quote: The protocol consists of an opening handshake followed by basic message framing, layered over TCP.

Rick Reed

quote: Raffi Krikorian explains the architecture used by Twitter to deal with thousands of events per sec - tweets, social graph mutations, and direct messages-.
author: Raffi Krikorian
note: InfoQ abstract. No transcript available, so none of the numbers below could be attributed verbatim to Krikorian himself.

quote: Twitter now has 150M world wide active users, handles 300K QPS to generate timelines, and a firehose that churns out 22 MB/sec.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: Twitter is primarily a consumption mechanism, not a production mechanism. 300K QPS are spent reading timelines and only 6000 requests per second are spent on writes.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: Tweet input statistics: 400m tweets per day; 5K/sec daily average; 7K/sec daily peak; >12K/sec during large events.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words. Not 4,600 avg as in the brief; the post says 5K/sec.

quote: Timeline delivery statistics: 30b deliveries / day (~21m / min); 3.5 seconds @ p50 (50th percentile) to deliver to 1m; 300k deliveries /sec; @ p99 it could take up to 5 minutes
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words. Looks transcribed from a slide.

quote: Completely precomputed home timeline. All the business rules get executed as tweets come in. Immediately the fanout process occurs. Tweets that come in are placed into a massive Redis cluster. Each tweet is replicated 3 times on 3 different machines.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: Your home timeline sits in a Redis cluster and is 800 entries long. If you page back long enough you'll hit the limit.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words. Entry = tweet ID, originating user ID, 4 bytes of flags.

quote: The tradeoff is fanout takes a little longer, but the read process is fast. About 2 seconds from a cold cache to the browser. For an API call it's about 400 msec.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: Twitter tries to do it under 5 seconds, but it doesn't always work, especially when celebrities tweet and tweet each other, which is happening more and more.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: 400 million tweets a day flow through the system and it can take up to 5 minutes for a tweet to flow from Lady Gaga's fingers to her 31 million followers.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: If you have 1 million followers it takes a couple of seconds to fanout all the tweets.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words.

quote: Not fanning out the high value users anymore. For people like Taylor Swift don't bother with fanout anymore, instead merge in her timeline at read time. Balances read and write paths. Saves 10s of percents of computational resources.
author: High Scalability (author slug 'hs', Todd Hoff's site; byline not shown), summarising Raffi Krikorian's talk
note: Blogger's summary of Krikorian's talk, not Krikorian's own words. Described as in progress ('Trying to figure out how to merge the read and write paths').

quote: The Aggregator: The query engine that accepts user queries and retrieves News Feed info from backend storage. It also does News Feed aggregation, ranking and filtering, and returns results to clients.
author: Yufei Zhu

quote: The Leaf: The distributed storage layer that indexes most recent News Feed actions and stores them in memory.
author: Yufei Zhu

quote: Tailer: The input data pipelines directs user actions and feedback into a leaf storage layer in real time.
author: Yufei Zhu

quote: Upon receiving a request, each aggregator fanned out the request to all the leaves to fetch data, rank and filter data, and return results to clients.
author: Yufei Zhu

quote: Each replica had 20 aggregators and 20 leaves.
author: Yufei Zhu

quote: By adjusting the ratio between the aggregators and leaves, we can reduce the overall CPU-to-RAM ratio from 20:20 to 20:5 or 20:4. This is a 75 percent to 80 percent reduction in RAM consumption.
author: Yufei Zhu

quote: Efficiency: 40% efficiency improvement via total memory and CPU consumption optimization for Multifeed Aggregator and Leaf infrastructure
author: Yufei Zhu
